question: What does a current of 1 ampere mean?
options: 1 volt of push across a wire
1 electron passing a point every second
1 joule of energy delivered each second
1 coulomb of charge passing a point every second
explanation: Current is charge per time: I = Q / t. One ampere is one coulomb per second, which is about 6.24e18 electrons per second.

question: When you flip a light switch, the lamp lights almost instantly. Why?
options: The wire is already full of free electrons; the push (the field) spreads along it at nearly light speed, so electrons everywhere start drifting at once
Electrons race from the switch to the lamp at the speed of light
The lamp stores electrons and releases them when the switch closes
The switch sends a radio signal to the lamp
explanation: Electrons only drift at about 0.1 mm/s. What travels fast is the change in the electric field, at roughly two thirds of the speed of light in a cable.

question: On a circuit diagram, current arrows point from + to - outside the battery. Which way do the electrons in the copper wire actually move?
options: The same way, from + to -
They do not move at all in a wire
The opposite way, from - to +
It depends on the colour of the wire
explanation: Franklin labelled the charges before anyone knew about electrons, and the label for electrons turned out to be negative. Conventional current (+ to -) is kept by agreement; electrons drift the other way.

question: A phone charger pushes 0.5 A for 10 minutes. How much charge has flowed?
options: 5 C
explanation: Convert the time first: 10 min = 600 s. Q = I x t = 0.5 x 600 = 300 C.

question: About how many electrons per second make up a 20 mA LED current? (e = 1.602e-19 C)
explanation: N = I / e = 0.020 / 1.602e-19 = 1.25e17 electrons per second.

question: Using v = I / (n e A) with n = 8.5e28 per m^3, roughly how fast do electrons drift for 1 A in a copper wire of 1 mm^2 cross-section?
options: About 300 000 km/s
About 1 m/s
About 0.07 mm/s
About 1 km/s
explanation: n e A = 8.5e28 x 1.602e-19 x 1e-6 = 1.36e4 C per metre. v = 1 / 1.36e4 = 7.3e-5 m/s, about 0.07 mm/s: slower than a snail.

question: A 2 A current flows through a thin wire, then a lamp, then a thick wire, all in one loop. What is the current in the thick wire?
options: Less than 2 A, because the lamp used some current
Exactly 2 A, the same as everywhere else in the single loop
More than 2 A, because thick wires carry more
Zero, because the lamp blocks it
explanation: Charge cannot pile up in a steady circuit, so the same charge per second passes every point of a single loop. The lamp takes energy, not charge. Only the drift speed differs: slower in the thick wire.

question: In an AC circuit at 50 Hz carrying about 1 A in ordinary copper wire, what do the electrons do?
options: Travel from the power station to your house and back each day
Stand completely still
Flow steadily from + to -
Wiggle back and forth in place by less than a micrometre
explanation: The current reverses 50 times a second, so each electron's slow drift keeps changing direction. The swing works out to about 0.33 micrometres. Energy is delivered even though the electrons go nowhere.
